articles.title: Every Drop Counts
articles.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 A2-B1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Water covers most of the Earth, but only a very small part of it is fresh water that people can drink. In dry seasons, some places do not have enough.
Saving water at home is easy. Turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. Take shorter showers. Fix leaks quickly, because a dripping tap can waste a lot of water in a year.
You can also reuse water. Water from washing vegetables can water your plants. Every drop counts. If everyone saves a little, together we can save a lot.

articles.title: Birds That Cannot Fly
articles.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 A2-B1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Penguins are birds, but they cannot fly. Instead, they are excellent swimmers. Their wings work like flippers and help them move quickly through the water to catch fish.
Most penguins live in the southern half of the world. Some live in very cold places like Antarctica, but others live on warmer coasts in South America and Africa.
Penguins often live in large groups. Parents take turns keeping their eggs warm and finding food. Today, some kinds of penguins are in danger because the oceans are changing.

articles.title: The Story of Paper
articles.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 A2-B1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Paper is so common that we rarely think about it. But for most of history, people wrote on stone, wood, cloth or animal skins.

Paper making was developed in ancient China about two thousand years ago. People mixed plant fibers with water, spread the mix thin and let it dry. Later, the idea slowly spread to other parts of the world.
Today, paper is made mostly from wood. Recycling paper saves trees, water and energy. Next time you finish with a newspaper or a box, put it in the recycling bin.

paras: Robert Waldinger leads a famous study that has followed people's lives for more than eight decades. In this later talk, he shares more of what the study has taught him.
The main message is simple but powerful: our relationships matter a lot for a happy and healthy life. Good relationships are like muscles. If we do not use them, they get weaker.
He suggests small actions to keep relationships strong, like sending a message to an old friend or having a real conversation with someone at work. Who could you contact this week?

b2.title: Why Every Drop of Water Counts
b2.zh: 為什麼每一滴水都重要
b2.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 B2 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Although water covers most of our planet, about 97 percent of it is salty seawater. Most of the fresh water is frozen in ice or hidden underground, which leaves only a tiny share that is easy for people to use.

Taiwan gets plenty of rain, but its rivers are short and steep, so much of the water flows quickly into the sea. During a severe drought in 2021, reservoirs fell to very low levels, and some areas had to limit their water supply.

Around the world, farming uses most of the fresh water we take, so saving water is not only about what happens at home. Still, small habits help: take shorter showers, fix dripping taps and reuse water from washing vegetables for your plants.

b2.title: Penguins: Birds Built for the Sea
b2.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 B2 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Penguins cannot fly, but they are superb swimmers. Their wings have become stiff flippers, and their smooth, torpedo-shaped bodies help them chase fish and squid underwater. Some species can dive hundreds of meters deep.

There are around 18 kinds of penguin, and almost all of them live in the Southern Hemisphere. Only a few live in Antarctica itself. Others live on the coasts of South America, Africa, Australia and New Zealand, and one species even lives near the equator in the Galápagos Islands.

Emperor penguins have one of the toughest lives on Earth. The males keep the egg warm on their feet through the dark Antarctic winter, without eating for weeks. Today, many penguin species are threatened by warming oceans, melting sea ice and overfishing.

b2.title: How Paper Changed the World
b2.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 B2 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Before paper became common, people wrote on materials such as bamboo, silk, clay and animal skins, which were heavy or expensive. Paper made from plant fibers was developed in ancient China, and an official named Cai Lun is traditionally credited with improving the method around 2,000 years ago.

Over many centuries, papermaking spread along trade routes to the Middle East and then to Europe. Combined with the printing press, cheap paper made books far more affordable and helped knowledge spread faster than ever before.

Most paper today is made from wood pulp. Recycling paper saves trees, water and energy, but paper fibers become shorter each time they are recycled, so they can only be reused a limited number of times.

b2.title: Relationships Need Exercise Too

source.name: TED：Robert Waldinger, The secret to a happy life: lessons from 8 decades of research

b2.note: 內容主題取自 TED 熱門演講。內文為學習用改寫，不是講者原話，請看原演講了解細節。
paras: Robert Waldinger directs the Harvard Study of Adult Development, which has followed people's lives for more than 80 years. In this later talk, he returns to the study's central finding: people with warmer relationships tend to be happier and healthier as they grow older.
Waldinger compares relationships to muscles. Just as our bodies need regular exercise, our connections with others need attention, or they slowly weaken. He calls this idea "social fitness".

The good news is that the steps can be very small. He encourages listeners to reach out to someone they have lost touch with, ask a colleague a real question, or simply put down their phone and listen. Small actions, repeated often, can keep important relationships strong.

c1.title: The Paradox of an Island Rich in Rain
c1.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 C1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Seen from space, Earth looks abundantly watery, yet the overwhelming majority of that water, about 97 percent, is saline. Of the small remainder that is fresh, most is locked in glaciers and ice caps or stored deep underground, leaving a strikingly thin margin readily available for human use.

Taiwan illustrates a paradox. Its annual rainfall is high by global standards, but the island's steep, short rivers rush much of that water to the sea within hours, and rainfall is concentrated in the plum-rain and typhoon seasons.

When typhoons failed to arrive in 2020, the island slid into one of its worst droughts in decades. By the following spring, reservoirs had dwindled to alarmingly low levels, prompting rationing in several regions and difficult trade-offs between farms, households and water-intensive industries.

Globally, agriculture accounts for the lion's share of freshwater withdrawals, which is why the most consequential savings often lie in efficient irrigation and leak-free distribution networks. Household habits matter too, but they work best alongside smarter infrastructure and pricing that reflects water's true scarcity.

c1.title: Masters of Two Worlds
c1.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 C1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Penguins forfeited flight long ago, but evolution compensated generously. Their wings have hardened into rigid flippers, dense bones counteract buoyancy, and streamlined bodies slip through water with remarkable efficiency. Emperor penguins can descend more than 500 meters in pursuit of prey, holding their breath for many minutes.

Contrary to popular imagery, penguins are not exclusively creatures of the ice. Of roughly eighteen species, only a handful breed on Antarctica itself; the rest inhabit sub-Antarctic islands and the coasts of South America, southern Africa, Australia and New Zealand. One species even nests on the equatorial Galápagos.

The emperor penguin's breeding cycle is among the most grueling in nature. Through the Antarctic winter, males incubate a single egg on their feet, huddling together against ferocious winds and fasting for weeks until the females return from the sea.

That dependence on a stable environment leaves many species precarious. Shrinking sea ice threatens the platforms emperors need to raise chicks, while warming waters, overfishing and pollution disrupt the food webs on which all penguins rely.

c1.title: A Material We Barely Notice
c1.zh: 我們幾乎沒注意到的材料
c1.note: 學習用短文，依參考資料改寫成 C1 程度，延伸閱讀請看來源連結。
paras: Paper is so ubiquitous that it has become almost invisible, yet for most of recorded history writing depended on far less convenient surfaces: clay tablets, bamboo strips, costly silk or parchment made from animal skin. Each constrained how much could be written and who could afford to do so.

The breakthrough came in China. Fragments of early paper predate him, but Cai Lun, an official of the Han court, is traditionally credited around 105 CE with refining a method of pulping plant fibers into thin, durable sheets.

The technique remained a closely held advantage for centuries before spreading westward along trade routes to the Islamic world, where paper mills flourished, and eventually to Europe. Paired with movable-type printing, abundant paper made books cheap enough to fuel mass literacy, the circulation of scientific ideas and the spread of religious and political debate.

The shift to wood pulp in the nineteenth century made paper cheaper still, at considerable cost to forests. Recycling now recovers much of what we use, though not indefinitely: each cycle shortens the fibers, which is why recycled paper typically requires an infusion of fresh pulp.

durable.def: able to last a long time

literacy.def: the ability to read and write

c1.title: The Practice of Social Fitness

source.name: TED：Robert Waldinger, The secret to a happy life: lessons from 8 decades of research

c1.note: 內容主題取自 TED 熱門演講。內文為學習用改寫，不是講者原話，請看原演講了解細節。
paras: Robert Waldinger has spent much of his career overseeing the Harvard Study of Adult Development, an investigation now spanning more than eight decades and, more recently, the children of its original participants. In this later talk, he revisits the study's most robust conclusion: the quality of our relationships is among the strongest predictors of health and happiness as we age.

What Waldinger adds here is a practical metaphor. Relationships, he suggests, behave like muscles. Neglect them and they atrophy; tend to them and they strengthen. Just as we accept that physical fitness requires ongoing effort, he argues that we should cultivate what he calls social fitness.

The framing is deliberately modest. Rather than demanding grand gestures, he points to small acts sustained over time: rekindling a lapsed friendship, asking a coworker a question that invites a genuine answer, giving someone our undivided attention.

Part of the talk's appeal is that it counters a pervasive myth, namely that connection should happen effortlessly. Waldinger's research suggests the opposite: lasting bonds are maintained deliberately, and it is never too late to begin.

oversee.def: to be in charge of work or people

investigation.g: an investigation spanning… 一項橫跨…的研究。

metaphor.def: describing something by comparing it to something else
metaphor.g: a practical metaphor 實用的比喻。

neglect.def: to not give enough care to something
neglect.g: Neglect them and… 忽略它們，就會…。

cultivate.g: cultivate social fitness 培養社交體能。

rekindle.def: to make a feeling or relationship start again
rekindle.g: rekindling a friendship 重拾友誼。

pervasive.g: a pervasive myth 普遍的迷思。

grammar.pt: 祈使句 + and 表條件
grammar.zh: Neglect them and… = 如果忽略它們，就…。
